column2: Having come to the place of torment, they suffer bitter and numbing pains. Raurava should be known as hot, its nature fierce with fiery heat;
and the one named Andha is ever painful with cold. Thus virtuous people, or righteous men in heaven, are very rare.
This reckoning has been fixed by the Lord, the Self-born; this count, derived from calculation, is Brahma's and not human.
The sages said: Mahar, Jana, Tapas, Satya, Bhuta, Bhavya and Bhava — these worlds and the spaces between them have been named by you.
Tell us truly what the intervals between the worlds are like. Hearing these words of the celibate sages, Vayu, who had seen the truth of things, spoke this truth.
Vayu said: The manifest is seen by reasoning; those who see directly see it through yoga,
and through withdrawal, meditation and austerity, the dissolution of the self. Ribhu, Sanatkumara and others, awakened and pure in intellect,
free of sheaths and of passion, good and supremely excellent, are Brahman itself; imperishable and full of joy, these yogins abide in Brahma's world.
As was done by those lords for the Valakhilya sages, just as I have seen it here while being present there.
The abode of the Lord is beyond the grasp of those whose purpose is unfulfilled; the Lord, being atomic, is grasped by the wise through inner feeling.
Knowledge, dispassion, lordship, austerity, truth, forbearance, steadfastness, the state of seer, relation to the self, and overlordship —
these ten imperishable qualities abide in Shankara. Being all-pervading and rich in yoga, he delights in favouring Brahma.
Taking a body as the world, he comes to help. The imperishable, fixed, undisturbed eighth is the one that arises by emanation.
The abode of that Lord is pure consciousness, supreme and made of maya; the god Maheshvara, master of maya, declares it made by maya.
The withdrawal of the gods and its measure are now declared; listen as I tell it in detail and in order.
Brahma's world is declared to be thirteen crores and ten niyutas of yojanas from the earthly world.
One crore of yojanas and fifty niyutas beyond Brahma's world is remembered as the upper part of the cosmic egg.
This is the upward extent, remembered as the furthest limit of movement. The natures, eternal and unmeasured, resting on one another's qualities,
subtle and productive, are then remembered as the Prakritis; from them was born the overseer, the knower of the field, called Brahma.
Among them, having Prakriti, is the subtle, imperishable overlordship — the unproduced supreme abode, the atom that rests in the Supreme.
He is imperishable and beyond inference, formless yet possessing form; appearance, disappearance, sustenance and grace are his.
The ordainer, incomparable to others, is the atomic great Lord; radiant, he illumines what lies before the darkness.
The golden egg that existed first, the emanated one, vast and round on all sides, arose from the Lord.
From the Lord comes the splitting of the seed; the knower of the field is regarded as the seed; Prakriti is declared the womb, and she has Narayana as her self.
The all-pervading one, for the creation of the world and the arrangement of the worlds — the emission from the true principle is the world-element of the great soul.
Beyond Brahma's world and within the egg of Brahma, between the two, is a divine city, made of mind and free from sickness.
It is the abode of the embodied Lord of boundless might; the city there named Shiva is the refuge of those who fear birth.
O best of brahmins, its inner extent is a full hundred thousand yojanas, set upon a circle like the earth.
With the light of the midday sun, overpowering all other splendour, and with a great golden rampart radiant as the sun,
with four golden gates adorned with strings of pearls, shining white like refined gold, it is well enclosed.
That lovely divine city in the sky resounds with bells and the like. In that finest and most delightful of cities, on its aerial terraces,
variegated with many jewels and filled with banners, rich in every desire and beautiful with groves and gardens,
in its houses of silver and of gold, like evening clouds and like Kailasa,
those devoted to Bhava, of good vows, rejoice on the tops of the fine palaces with delightful enjoyments of sound and the other senses.
The sounds of Vedic recitation are unceasing, with many auspicious stories, and the sounds of song and instruments flow all around;
incomparable gatherings take place, and such things go on upon the tops of their palaces.
There is a beautiful thousand-pillared palace of refined gold, adorned everywhere with incomparable fine jewels —
with crystals like the moon, with the lustre of beryl gems, with gold like the morning sun and with the brilliance of fire.
Hearing this, the ascetic sages of Naimisha cried out, and, falling into doubt, spoke these words to the Wind.
The sages said: Who are those great souls devoted to Bhava who, most worthy of grace, rejoice fully in that finest of cities?
Hearing the sages' words, Vayu spoke: Hear of those by whom devotion to the god of gods has been cultivated:
the modest, the vigorous, the self-controlled, the courageous and the free from greed, who with pure inner self in deed, mind and speech,
single-minded, have taken refuge in Maheshvara — they have obtained residence in Rudra's world, the eternal, imperishable state.
They attain the unsurpassed likeness of Bhava's form: all with faces like fire, of universal form, with matted locks,
blue-throated, dark-necked, with sharp fangs and three eyes, crowned with the crescent moon and wearing crowns of matted hair,
all ten-armed heroes, fragrant as the inside of a lotus, like the rising sun, all clad in yellow,
all bearing the Pinaka bow in hand, riding white bulls, glorious, wearing earrings and adorned with pearl necklaces,
with bodies surpassing in splendour, omniscient and all-seeing; dividing themselves in many ways, free from old age and death,
they sport in various states, enjoying pleasures most rare, moving at will, perfected, and enlightened by other perfected ones.
There are many crores of the great-souled eleven Rudras. With them the great-souled god of gods, Maheshvara,
the Lord compassionate to his devotees, beloved of Parvati, rejoices. I see no difference between those Rudras and the great-souled Bhava;
I tell you this truly. So spoke Matarishvan this holy account, heard from the Lord.
Then all those sages, radiant as the sun, having heard this supreme and holy story of the three-eyed god,
having received great grace and unsurpassed joy, honoured Vayu of great strength and spoke to him.
The sages said: O glorious Wind, O lord, you have told us of the Lord's supreme, holy eighth emanation,
and properly described his abode and its measure, rich in the dharma of yoga, the supreme abode of the Supreme Self.
The greatness of Mahadeva is hard to know even for the gods, by his own greatness and yoga, the thousandfold one of boundless might.
His bewildering of his devotees is only for the sake of compassion. The splendour of Brahma, attended by Lakshmi herself, incomparable,
pervading like the moonlight of the moon, is placed in the universal form; that glory shines exceedingly in the dwelling of the god of gods,
and of the great-souled Rudras equal to Mahadeva. All of this, entirely, has flowed like nectar from your mouth,
and we have drunk it with devotion to Sharva, O one of good vows. There is nothing else unknown; now, O breath of the best of gods, please answer our question properly.
Suta said: The Lord then said, "What more shall I describe? Whatever I ought to tell, that I shall tell, O you of good vows."
The sages said: The Adityas at his side, the lions of wrathful valour, the Vaishvanaras, the hosts of beings and the tigers that follow him —
in the terrible dissolution of beings, at the destruction of all living creatures, what becomes of them? Tell us truly.
Having understood the nature of the Lord and the unmanifest source, Vayu said: Where the young sons of Brahma went before —
Sanandana, Sanaka, and the third, Sanatana, Vodhu, Kapila among them, and the illustrious Asuri,
the sage Panchashikha and others like them — then, when time has passed and the cycle of kalpas has gone round,
at the end of the destruction of the great elements, when dissolution is at hand, the many crores of Rudras, who have propitiated the great Goddess,
abandoning the enjoyments of sound and the other objects and the eightfold support, entering all beings with a splendour joined to knowledge,
leaving the undisturbed station out of compassion for beings — there the great souls go to the atomic Maheshvara.
They cross the river of great whirlpools whose waters are birth and death; then they behold the undivided, supreme Brahman.
Together with the Goddess are the seven who are declared goddesses; the thousand lions and likewise the Adityas,
the Vaishvanaras, the hosts of beings and the tigers that follow him — drawing all of them into himself, along with those fit to be counted,
these seven worlds again and the five great elements — joined with Vishnu, he creates and transforms.
That Rudra consists of the Samans and likewise of the Yajus; he is woven through and across, outside and inside, certainly.
The Lord and master is one, the origin and the ender, O twice-born. Then all those sages, radiant as the sun,
having properly placed the fire within themselves by true hearing, with pure inner self in deed, mind and speech,
single-minded, take refuge in Maheshvara, devoted to vows and fasts, intent on compassion for all beings.
They, their doubts cut off, attained the divine unsurpassed yoga; taking refuge with supreme devotion and with splendour joined to knowledge,
they obtained residence in Rudra's world, the eternal, imperishable state. Whoever, joined with austerity, recites this revelation declared by Vayu —
whether brahmin, kshatriya or vaishya, devoted to his own duties — attains Rudra's world, the cause of the world.
When creation has ceased and all rests in Prakriti, then, because it is utterly beyond perception and unseen by anyone,
indescribable, unknowable, unknown even to the wise, and because it comes and goes, there is no grasping of it.
What is said here is said after reflecting by inference from what is grasped by feeling. When that cause, eternal, of the nature of being and non-being, abides,
indefinable, activity arises from its own nature as cause. Thus the Prakritis, repeated twice seven times in order,
enter into one another at the withdrawal of creation. The egg by which all this is covered dissolves into the waters —
the seven worlds with their mountains, ending with the seven continents and oceans. The covering of water dissolves into light;
the covering of light the wind swallows; the covering of wind space swallows;
the covering of space the Bhutadi swallows; and the Mahat, whose mark is intellect, swallows the Bhutadi.
The unmanifest, the equilibrium of the qualities beyond it, swallows the Mahat. These two, withdrawal and expansion, are Brahma manifest again;
he creates and swallows through modification at creation and withdrawal. The perfected knowers, whose effects and instruments are accomplished,
having attained swiftness and dissolved into their own places, the knowers of the field are yoked again to their instruments at the withdrawal.
The unmanifest is called the field, and Brahma is called the knower of the field. Their union, made by likeness and unlikeness, is beginningless.
Thus, O brahmins, it is to be understood among the knowers of the field in the creations; the knower of Brahman should be known as distinct from the knower of the field.
The field and its knower are remembered as object and non-object: Brahma should be known as non-object, and the field is called object.
The field governed by its knower is declared to exist for the knower. Because bodies are many, the embodied one is remembered as manifold.
And the light that abides undivided in Shankara — since pleasure and pain are experienced in each body,
therefore the plurality of persons should be understood by the discerning. When the restraint of these distinctions comes about,
all, impelled by their own nature, then turn back in the great course of time; those of the Self-born whose passions are stilled,
together with all who have attained union and dwell in Brahma's world, when their state of dwelling in the self ceases,
for those dwelling there at that time who see faults, dispassion arises that destroys the notion of an individual self.
Seeing that state through the diversity of enjoyer and enjoyed, the knowers of the field in Brahma's world, through discriminating knowledge,
all beyond cause in Prakriti, seeing diversity, abide in their own self, tranquil and of the nature of pure seeing.
All pure and stainless, conscious and non-conscious alike, they attain final nirvana there and are remembered as not returning.
Being without qualities and without individual self, they pass beyond Prakriti at its end. Thus the elemental re-dissolution has been declared by the Self-born.
Whoever, observing the conduct of his class and stage of life, hears of the re-dissolution, devoted and free from fever, goes to residence in Shiva's world.
A Shudra who does not drink liquor, who is devoted to Bhava and self-controlled, remaining until the dissolution of beings and marked by being unobstructed,
obtains leadership of Shiva's hosts or an abiding place. One who drinks liquor rejoices with drinkers and with hosts of spirits.
Bhava, served on the surface of the earth, grants boons to mortals. Thus spoke the Lord Vayu these excellent words.
That state into which the embodied go is called 'avastha'. The sin and merit of creatures that is established in Prakriti —
those very merits and sins, abiding in their states, yoke creatures again to bodies, in this world and beyond.
The dharma and adharma of creatures, both consisting only of qualities, are accumulated by creatures here as bodies through their own causes.
The conscious qualities governed by the knower of the field dissolve; in creation, re-dissolution and worldly existence, creatures
are joined and separated and move about through their causes. The modes of activity — rajasic, tamasic and sattvic —
consisting of qualities, proceed in three ways, governed by the Person. Sattva has the nature of the upper region; tamas that of the lower part;
rajas, which sets both in motion, turns about here in the middle. Thus the three, consisting of the qualities of mind, revolve.
The one who knows should not act on these among all beings in the worlds. Undertakings rooted in ignorance are begun by men.
These three courses are remembered as ranging from auspicious to sinful. Overcome by tamas, a creature does not find the truth.
Through not seeing reality, he is then bound in various ways: by the natural bond and by the bond of modification,
and bound by the third, of sacrificial fees, he turns about endlessly. These are declared the three bonds, caused by ignorance.
Taking the impermanent as permanent, seeing pleasure in pain, thinking what is not one's own to be one's own, and judging the impure to be pure —
those who have these faults of mind are in error through reversed knowledge. The cessation of attraction and aversion is declared to be knowledge.
Ignorance is the root of tamas; rajas is the fruit of the two kinds of action; from action comes rebirth in a body, and great suffering proceeds.
Born of the ear, the eye, the skin, the tongue and the nose, thirst arises from action and suffering, causing rebirth.
The thirsting fool, driven by the fruits of his own actions, turns round and round in that very place like an oil-press ox.
Therefore ignorance is taught to be the root of all evils; recognising it as the one enemy, one should strive for knowledge.
Through knowledge one renounces everything; through renunciation the mind becomes dispassionate; through dispassion one is purified; and, purified, one is freed by sattva.
Next I shall speak of passion, which carries beings away. For the uncontrolled, it leads to attachment to the objects of sense:
the unwelcome and the welcome, dislike and liking, torment and dejection, distress at meeting pain and longing memory of pleasure.
This passion for sense-objects is remembered as the cause of birth in the elemental world, from Brahma down to the plants.
It is preceded by ignorance; therefore one should give up ignorance. One who does not accept the authority of the sages or the conduct of the cultured,
who acts against the order of classes and stages of life and opposes the scriptures of the wise — this path is the cause of hell and of animal birth.
That is declared the cause of going to an animal womb: threefold in the place of torment and sixfold among animal births.
There is obstruction everywhere in cause and object; all that lack of power is remembered as consisting of obstruction.
This is the fourfold tamasic course of beings. The mind resting purely in sattva shows things as they truly are.
Having seen the principles as they are through the vision of truth, the distinction between sattva and the knower of the field — this is the vision of distinct things.
The vision of distinction is knowledge, and from knowledge comes what is called yoga. Through it the bondage of the bound, and through it the release of the freed.
When worldly existence has ceased, the freed one is released from the subtle body; without connection and without mental activity, he abides in his own self.
Even abiding in the self, he is described as formless. Thus the characteristics of knowledge and liberation have been told in brief.
That liberation is declared threefold by those who see the truth: first, separation through knowledge; second, through the destruction of passion;
third, through the destruction of craving — thus the cause of liberation is explained. From the absence of the subtle body comes isolation, and from isolation, stainlessness.
Through stainlessness one is pure; there is no other beyond this. Next I shall speak of dispassion arising from seeing faults.
Toward objects of the five kinds, divine and human alike, one should practise freedom from aversion and from attachment by seeing their faults.
One should give up torment, pleasure and dejection. Adopting dispassion in this way, the embodied one becomes free of possessiveness.
Reflecting with the intellect that it is impermanent, inauspicious and painful, the effects and instruments become purified through intense cultivation of sattva.
One whose impurities have ripened sees all faults. Then at the time of departure, through faults and occasioning causes,
the heat in the body, aroused and driven by fierce wind, resting in the body, obstructs all the humours.
Breaking the seats of life and cutting through the vital points, the wind aroused by cold then rises upward.
It abides in the seats of life of all beings. When, in short, knowledge is shut off and actions have come to an end,
that individual soul, whose support is the navel, through its own former actions again causes the eightfold operation of the breath to depart.
At the end, abandoning the body, it becomes breathless; thus abandoned by the vital breaths, one is called dead.
As in this world one is led here and there in a dream, so is its colouring for the one subject to it; there is nothing else.
The third is the destruction of craving; thus the mark of liberation is explained. Seeing faults in the fivefold objects beginning with sound,
freedom from aversion and attachment, and giving up pleasure and torment — these are the causes of dispassion and of the dissolution of the Prakritis.
The eight Prakritis described earlier should be known in order; those beginning with the unmanifest and ending with the elements should be known as products of Prakriti.
One who observes the conduct of his class and stage of life, cultured and not opposed to scripture — this dharma of the classes and stages is the cause of attaining divine abodes.
From Brahma down to the Pishachas there are eight stations of the deities; lordship beginning with the power of becoming minute is the eightfold cause.
The cause lies in non-obstruction, seen with the marks of sound and the rest; these eight forms of Prakriti are in order.
Consisting only of qualities, they attach themselves to the knowers of the field. As those with eyes see a separate cloud in the rainy season,
so such perfected ones see the soul with divine sight — eating food and drink and entering wombs,
running across, above and below in turn. Soul, breath, subtle body and instrument — this fourfold group
is described by synonymous words of one meaning. This one, of manifest and unmanifest measure, experiences everything completely.
Whatever ends in the grace of the unmanifest and is governed by the knower of the field — knowing this and becoming pure, one is freed through knowledge.
When the reality of the principles has vanished through the vision of truth, when the body breaks, he departs at will, wholly at peace.
Then the instrument of the knower of the unmanifest also breaks; freed from the body of qualities, from the breath and the rest entirely,
he does not take another body, just as a sprout does not arise from a burnt seed. The knower, having understood all worldly existence, body and mind,
awakened by knowledge to the fourteen, established in Prakriti, turns back. They call Prakriti the true and its modification the false.
Non-being should be known as falsehood, and being is called truth. They declare the knower of the field to be without name and form, while the field has name and form.
Because he knows the field, he is called the knower of the field; because he perceives the field, the knower of the field is called auspicious.
Therefore he is remembered as the knower of the field, and the field is so described by those who know it. The field is seen as dependent on him; the knower of the field is always the perceiver.
Because it wastes away, because it is a cause, because it protects from injury, and because it is to be enjoyed and is an object, the knowers of the field call it the field.
From the Mahat down to the particulars, of every form and distinct, its mark is modification; that imperishable one goes to the perishable.
Because it flows away again after each modification, and for that reason, it is called perishable.
Because it protects a person in worldly existence and from the hells, and again because it protects from suffering, it is called the field.
Because of pleasure, pain and the sense of I, it is called the enjoyable; being non-conscious it is the object, and the all-pervading one is remembered as of different nature.
That which spreads out as modification neither wastes nor flows away; therefore it is also called imperishable, since it does not decay.
Because he lies within the city of the body, he is called Purusha; because he is the one who perceives the city, he is called Purusha.
Tell of the Purusha — he is described by the ignorant as told. He is pure, stainless in appearance, the knower, yet devoid of knowledge.
Whether he is or is not, whether other, bound or free, gone or staying — being causeless and indefinable, there is no 'I' in him.
Being pure he is not seen; being the seer, he sees equally. Because he causes self-awareness, he is not lessened and is without cause.
Reflecting by inference on what is grasped by feeling, one is not deluded. When one sees the knower, tranquil in aim and of the nature of seeing,
indicated among the visible and invisible, then that is excellent and hard to hold. The knower is not seen here separately in any way.
The self whose nature is the cause restrains the self by its own self; there, in Prakriti the cause, it abides in its own self.
Whether he is or is not, whether other, here or hereafter, one or separate, the knower of the field or the Person,
whether self or non-self, conscious or non-conscious, doer or non-doer, enjoyer or the enjoyed —
having reached the stainless knower of the field, they do not return. It is inexpressible because it cannot be told, and ungraspable by arguments;
beyond reasoning because inconceivable and unattainable in every way; the truth cannot be spoken by speech, nor reached along with the mind.
When the knower of the field is without qualities, pure, tranquil, dissolved, stainless, beyond pleasure and pain, restrained and come to peace,
in that selfless one there is neither the expressible nor the inexpressible. These two, withdrawal and expansion, are then the manifest and unmanifest again.
It is created and swallowed, and it rests in the manifest; all that is governed by the knower of the field proceeds again in creation.
At its end it resorts to its support, preceded by intellect. The union of the two, made by likeness and unlikeness, is known; this beginningless union is remembered as born of the Great Person.
As long as the time of creation and dissolution lasts, so long the world stands, held in check. It proceeds first, preceded by intellect, only for the sake of the Person.
This, marked by creation and dissolution, whether arising from Pradhana or caused by the Lord, beginningless and endless, preceded by self-conceit, comes upon the world, terrifying it.
This is the elemental creation, the third, marked by cause. Having understood this, one is then freed forever.
Thus I have told you the threefold re-dissolution in detail and in order. What more shall I describe?

As you, having duly worshipped the gods and others and attained the concluding bath, are purified, so, abandoning your bodies at the end of life, your purpose fulfilled, may you reach the holy world and rejoice.
Those sages of Naimisha, having seen and touched it, bathed in the concluding bath, and all the participants in the sacrificial session went to heaven.
So you too, O brahmins, having performed many kinds of sacrifices, will go to heaven at the end of your lives, O best of the twice-born.
The Prakriya is the first quarter, the beginning of the story; then the Anushanga, the Upodghata and the Upasamhara.
Thus this four-quartered Purana, esteemed by the world, was spoken by the Lord Vayu himself, devoted to the welfare of the world,
to the sages at the sacrificial session in Naimisha, O best of sages — perfected by his grace, dealing with the origin and dissolution of beings.
Having properly understood this creation arising from Pradhana and caused by the Lord, the wise one does not fall into delusion.
The learned brahmin who hears this ancient history, or causes it to be heard, or teaches it,
rejoices for endless years in the abodes of great Indra; attaining union with Brahma, he rejoices with Brahma.
Proclaiming the fame of those famous, great-souled lords of creatures and lords of the earth, he goes to oneness with Brahman.
This Purana, told by Krishna Dvaipayana, expounder of Brahman, brings blessings, fame and long life, is holy and equal to the Vedas.
Whoever spreads this fame of the lords of the Manu periods, and of the gods and sages of abundant wealth and splendour,
is freed from all sins and obtains great merit. And the learned one who always causes this to be heard on each festival day,
his sins shaken off and heaven won, becomes fit for oneness with Brahman. Whoever at a shraddha causes brahmins to hear even a quarter of it,
that offering becomes imperishable and fulfils every wish, and it reaches the ancestors. Because it breathes of ancient times, it is called Purana.
Whoever knows its etymology is freed from all sins. Likewise the men of the three classes who study it,
and who, having heard this history, set their minds on dharma — as many pores as there are on their bodies,
for that many thousands of crores of years they rejoice in heaven; attaining union with Brahma, they rejoice with the gods.
This holy, purifying and glorious Purana, removing all sins, Brahma gave to Matarishvan.
From him it was received by Ushanas, and from him by Brihaspati; Brihaspati then told it to Savitri.
Savitri told it to Death, and Death to Indra; Indra to Vasishtha, and he to Sarasvata.
Sarasvata told it to Tridhaman, Tridhaman to Sharadvat; Sharadvat gave it to Trivishta and to Antariksha.
Antariksha gave it to Charshin, and he to Trayyaruna; from Trayyaruna Dhananjaya received it, and he gave it to Kritanjaya.
From Kritanjaya it went to Trinanjaya, and from him to Bharadvaja; Bharadvaja gave it to Gautama, and he to Niryantara.
Niryantara told it to Vajashravas; he gave it to Somashushma, and he gave it to Trinabindu.
Trinabindu told it to Daksha, and Daksha to Shakti; from Shakti, Parashara heard it while still in the womb.
From Parashara it went to Jatukarnya, and from him to the lord Dvaipayana; and from Dvaipayana I received it, O best of the twice-born.
And I have told it again to my son of boundless intelligence. Thus the words of the teachers beginning with Brahma have been set forth.
The teachers should be saluted with care by the wise. This brings blessings, fame and long life, is holy and accomplishes every aim.
Destroying sin, it should always be heard by brahmins with discipline. It should not be given to the impure, the sinful, or one who has not stayed for a year,
nor to one without faith, the unlearned, or one without a son in any way, nor to one who is hostile; this is supremely purifying.

He whose source they declare to be the unmanifest, whose body is the manifest, who is time and the goal; fire is his mouth, the moon and sun his eyes, the directions his ears, and they call the wind his breath;
the Vedas are his speech, the atmosphere his body, the earth his feet, the stars the pores of his skin; all the heavens his heads, and the sciences and Upanishads his tail —
to that god of gods, the begetter of beings, whose self is sacrifice, established in the Satya world, best of the best, giver of boons, the great Lord, Brahma the first, I bow with devotion.
Let my teaching be spread in the worlds by you, great souls who are the teachers of all beings; this is my wish.
I am the beginning of beings, the first maker, the Lord himself, the agent of all creation, sustenance and dissolution.
Threefold in form, beyond the three qualities, without qualities yet the support of qualities,
moving at will, the self of beings, consisting of Pradhana and Purusha — thus, O Brahman, is my nature, who bear the form of the three worlds.
My form became twofold, as Pradhana and Purusha. My form as Pradhana consists of the qualities of all the worlds;
the other, beyond the qualities, is great, higher than the highest. Knowing these two in this way, one is freed — what then of both?
Through long austerities, restraints and observances, and through renunciation, when evil deeds are destroyed, liberation is quickly obtained.
The form endowed with qualities is attained through oneness with those qualities; the other, the form of the whole world, consists of action, enjoyment and effort.
That is attained through actions, and it is also attained through renouncing them; but renunciation of both is hard for all, O ascetic.
It is imperishable and easy to reach, within the range of good and bad actions,
by the quality that dwells in the self, whether good or bad; the knowledge that comes through oneness with the self grants all perfections.
Even for the most sinful men outside the three classes, by merely meditating on this form, evil deeds turn into good.
Those who worship the supreme Shakti, with rites or without, are surely not bound to worldly existence; they are freed, without doubt.
Shiva, having worshipped her through the power of meditation and yoga, became the lord of all the perfected ones, the Lord who is half woman.
Other gods led by the lotus-born became perfected through the power of meditating on her. Therefore, for all the worlds, without worship of Tripura
neither enjoyment nor liberation is found anywhere together. With mind fixed on her, breath absorbed in her, worshipping her, all your acts directed to her,
performing actions in identity with her, you will attain liberation. This secret has been told out of desire for the good of all,
by me, pleased with your austerity, O best of sages. May gods, sages, perfected ones, men and others obtain from the lotus of your mouth the perfection beyond the highest.
Hearing these words of Hayagriva, the bearer of the Sharnga bow, he bowed and again spoke to Madhusudana:
O Lord, what is the nature of that form you spoke of before? What is its play and what its power? Please tell me this.
Hayagriva said: "O divine sage, this Hayagriva is my other self, a portion of me; whatever you wish to hear, he will tell you all."
Having instructed the ascetic Hayagriva thus, Hari, lord of the world, vanished before the pot-born sage.
Then the ascetic, filled with wonder and with hair standing on end, returned to his hermitage with the sage Hayagriva.

For the killing of a king, a twice-born, a Vedic scholar, one learned in the Veda, a vowed ascetic, a knower of Vedanta and knowers of the Veda, the good declare expiations of one, two, fifty and ten thousand in turn.

In protecting them and in giving gifts to them, they declare the merit to be as described before, increasing in the same order — likewise in seeing them, bowing to them, doing their work and serving them.
Lions, tigers, deer and others that harm people the king should always kill, for the sake of the gods and of brahmins;
and in times of distress, even for his own sake, he may kill and eat animals that are ritually pure.
One should not cook food for oneself alone, nor cook animals for oneself alone; one who cooks for the gods or for brahmins is not tainted.
Long ago, the blessed Maya, intent on bringing the world to life, created all the gods, and likewise Asuras and men,
and for their protection also fourteen kinds of animals; having made the sacrifices and their rules, she said to them:
O men, worship the gods with animals by this rule. Those who give offerings, nourished and made prosperous by sacrifice —
whoever here does not follow the wheel thus set in motion becomes poor and goes to hell, birth after birth.
For the gods and the ancestors, for a guest, for a teacher and on the arrival of a great person, the twice-born may kill ritually pure animals.
In times of distress a brahmin who eats pure meat incurs no fault. One should do what is enjoined and avoid what is forbidden.
Long ago there was a great sacrifice of the gods held by Yuvanashva; a quarrel arose among the gods, each saying, "This is mine."
Then Brahma, grandsire of the worlds, apportioned men and animals among the gods, dividing them one by one.
Then the supreme Shakti, helper of the multitude of beings, became angry; Brahma, full of prudence, spoke to her.
Seeing her appear, filled with fear for the welfare of beings, he bowed with joined palms and praised her, saying again and again, "Be gracious!"

Since you have appeared before me, I am fulfilled. All this action, good and bad, has been fashioned by you.
brahmandpuran:118:64	The Shrutis and the Smritis have been set forth by you alone; the sacrifices in the great rite were devised by you through my mouth.
brahmandpuran:118:65	The animals that were apportioned to the gods, O supreme Goddess, let them all be yours, for the satisfaction of beings as well.
Having said this, the Grandsire vanished before their very eyes; and by the rule he had stated he performed great sacrifices,
and worshipped the supreme Shakti, offering ritually pure animals. Their apportionment is not stated here since it is declared in the Vedas.
Women and Shudras may take meat without a brahmin; in times of distress a brahmin too may eat it with his teacher's permission.

This body born of Shiva has now attained the state of Shiva. Awaken, O animal; you are not inauspicious but auspicious.
brahmandpuran:118:70	The Lord is the maker of the whole world, its origin and its dissolution; since Rudra surpasses the universe, you, O animal, are Rudra.
With this, having killed a horse, cow, elephant, camel, buffalo or the like, for oneself or for another, one is not tainted by fault;

or harmful creatures of the house — snakes, rats, scorpions and the like. This is for householders who seek the fruit of their rites, and for the great ones of Shiva's splendour whose mental resolves are fulfilled.
For others, animal sacrifice brings fulfilment of their wishes; but for those great ones their wishes are accomplished through recitation, fire offerings, worship and the like.
All this has been done out of compassion by you, O best of brahmins. The brahmins led by Devavrata accepted it in the same way,
and the great-souled, mighty ones, content in mind, gave him the name Dvijavarman and her the name Shilavati.
For their protection the self-controlled man, together with his kinsmen, joyfully made his dwelling there with his wife.
Pleasing all the brahmins, he named this city Devaratapura after the name of the family priest.
Then in the course of time Dvijavarman died, and the messengers of Yama, Brahma, Vishnu and Rudra came.
A battle arose among them like that of gods and Asuras. Meanwhile the sage Narada arrived and said:

Do not fight one another; listen to my words. This hunter formerly built a causeway with stolen wealth.
brahmandpuran:119:41	He must wander alone as a wind-spirit until the death of the owners of the wealth; he took wealth from many, so until their deaths likewise.
When all the messengers had gone, having heard Narada's words, he wandered for twelve years as a wind-spirit in the sky.
The sage said to his wife, "You have no fault at all; by the merit you have earned, go from here to Brahma's world."
Seeing her husband as a wind-spirit, she did not wish for Brahma's abode; filled with deep despondency, she spoke thus to the sage:

I will not go to the Grandsire without my husband. I will stay here until my husband regains his own body.
brahmandpuran:119:46	Then whatever course he takes, I will follow. Or is there some remedy that I or he should perform?
Hearing her words, the ascetic was pleased and said: "Your body is made for enjoyment, and your actions bring results.
By my power it will come about; I shall tell you the remedy. Fasting, bathing daily at a great holy place, worshipping Shiva with Amba,
worshipping Shiva with devotion and eating bulbs, roots and fruits, meditating on the great Lord in the heart, one should recite the Shatarudra hymn.
By a thousand and eight recitations even the slayer of a brahmin is freed from sin; one is freed from all other sins as well, without doubt."
Having instructed her thus, the ascetic gave her the Rudradhyaya; having blessed that woman, he vanished right there.
For her husband's sake she resolved and performed that supreme recitation; freed from the sin of theft, he regained his own body.
Then the thief named Vajra died, and the others who owned that wealth also died.
Yama summoned them and spoke these words:
You have committed sin, and by chance also some good. Which fruit do you wish to enjoy first — that of the evil or of the good?
